The other triggers, threats, appraisals, and strategies center on interpersonal closeness, malevolent intent, bodily vulnerability, and interpersonal hypervigilance; cycling stands out as a highly specific cue without support elsewhere in the formulation.

vignette:
The assault happened thirty-seven years ago, in the parking lot behind her field station in northern Montana. Eleanor had been cataloging soil samples well past dusk, a habit she'd never questioned. When a man she recognized from a nearby ranch cornered her between two trucks, she froze. She remembered thinking, If I don't fight, it will be over faster. That thought-that she had chosen passivity, that her own stillness had been a form of complicity-had calcified into a belief she could not shake: the event happened because of the way she acted. She had come to believe that her body, in its stillness, had betrayed her, and she felt a deep, lingering shame for what had been done to it.

Now seventy-seven and living alone in a small apartment in Portland, Eleanor had retired from environmental consulting but still worked part-time analyzing water samples for a local nonprofit. The work kept her indoors, in a lab with no windows, which she preferred. Open or exposed spaces made her feel vulnerable, and she avoided them whenever possible. Even a walk to the corner store required a route that kept buildings on both sides-a corridor she could navigate without feeling seen. She had also stopped making eye contact with people, especially men, because she was certain that any glance could be misread, that it invited a kind of attention she could not risk. What frightened her most was that you could never know who would harm you; the man in the parking lot had been someone she'd waved to a dozen times.

This belief-that danger was invisible and arbitrary-kept her scanning every room she entered. She always identified escape routes before she felt comfortable anywhere, a habit so automatic it felt like breathing. In the lab, she chose the bench closest to the back exit. At the grocery store, she positioned her cart so she could see the door. Sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard; a coworker reaching for a file too quickly could make her flinch. At home, she listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering, checking the lock three times before bed. This constant vigilance wore her down, and it also fed her shame: A normal person wouldn't live like this. The more she avoided, the more she believed she had something to be ashamed of, and the more she felt the need to keep watching.

Sexual situations or intimacy were unthinkable. She had not been on a date in decades. Physical affection such as hugs made her stiffen; even a well-meaning touch on the shoulder from a colleague could send her heart racing. Being alone with a man-any man, even her elderly neighbor who needed help carrying groceries-was something she arranged around, always ensuring a third person was present or the encounter was brief and in a public corridor. These triggers were not random; they were the direct expression of her conviction that harm could come from anyone, at any time, and that her own past actions had made her a target.

The loop tightened over the years. Her avoidance of open spaces meant she stopped hiking, which had been her greatest joy. Her refusal to be alone with male colleagues limited the projects she could take on, and eventually she stopped applying for fieldwork altogether. She dwelled on how the event could have been prevented-If I had left at sunset. If I had parked closer. If I had screamed.-and each replay deepened her self-blame. The more she ruminated, the more she watched for threats, and the more she watched, the more she found evidence that the world was dangerous. She was certain that her vigilance was the only thing keeping her safe, and yet it was also the thing that made her feel perpetually unsafe.

What finally brought Eleanor to seek help was a practical crisis: her landlord had hired a new maintenance man, a young man with a kind face, and she could not bring herself to let him into her apartment to fix the leak under her sink. She had gone without water for three days, boiling pasta water to wash with, before she called a clinic. She was most afraid that therapy would confirm what she already believed-that she was too old to change, that the damage was permanent. But she was also tired. She said, "I don't want to spend the rest of my life checking the locks."
